common_name: Bradenton Loquat (Vigorous Large-Fruited Tropical Florida Loquat)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown grafted tree in spring in full to partial sun in well-drained soil; Bradenton is among the least cold-hardy loquat selections, so it performs best in warm coastal microclimates and should be sited with wind and freeze protection in mind.

directions: Give Bradenton a warm, sheltered site with excellent drainage, since it is one of the more tropical-leaning loquat selections and reacts poorly to hard freezes compared to older Florida cultivars. The stout, bushy tree bears at a young age and produces large, roughly two-inch, sweet fruit with good flavor, ripening late in the loquat season into April. In frost-free microclimates it can flush repeated small crops through the year rather than a single spring harvest, a trait growers sometimes call 'everbearing.' Thin dense fruit clusters to improve fruit size, and prune lightly after harvest to keep this naturally compact tree manageable in a small Gulf Coast yard.

planting.note: Grow in a container or well-drained garden bed in full sun; Procimequat stays naturally small and precocious, fruiting heavily even as a young potted plant, so it suits Gulf Coast gardeners who want a movable citrus for hard-freeze nights.

directions: Procimequat was bred by crossing Eustis limequat with Hong Kong kumquat (Fortunella hindsii) to combine tart lime flavor with the tiny, ornamental fruiting habit of the wild kumquat parent. The naturally dwarf plant is a triploid, so it rarely if ever sets viable seed, but it flowers and fruits abundantly regardless, covering itself in small, pale orange, marble-sized fruit useful more for pickling, garnish, and ornamental interest than fresh eating. Keep it in a container of well-drained citrus mix in full sun and bring it under cover during hard freezes, since this rare hybrid is grown almost entirely by citrus collectors rather than commercial growers. Light, frequent feeding with citrus fertilizer through the growing season keeps the compact plant productive.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in full sun and sharply drained soil; Yuzuquat's cold hardiness, inherited from its yuzu parent, makes it one of the more reliable lemon-flavored citrus choices for Gulf Coast gardens where true lemons struggle.

directions: Yuzuquat is a tri-generic hybrid, developed by Texas citrus breeder John Brown, combining hardy yuzu with 'Nagami' kumquat to produce a small tree far tougher than any true lemon. It carries fragrant spring flowers followed by egg-sized, sour, aromatic fruit that substitutes well for lemon in cooking and drinks, with juice and zest both usable in the kitchen. The compact, glossy-leaved evergreen tree suits a sheltered full-sun spot in the ground in zone 9a, or a large container that can be moved to cover on the rare hard-freeze night. Reduce watering during winter dormancy and keep soil sharply drained year-round to avoid root problems in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
